Evaluate the accuracy and efficiency on the test data set 1. Introduction A Decision Tree is a supervised machine learning algorithm used for both classification and regression tasks. It works by splitting the dataset into smaller subsets based on feature values, eventually resulting in a tree-like structure of decisions. 2. Structure of a Decision Tree Root Node: Represents the entire dataset and the first decision. Decision Nodes: Internal nodes where the dataset is split based on a feature condition. Leaf Nodes (Terminal Nodes): Represent the final output (class label for classification or value for regression). Branches: Arrows that connect nodes, representing the outcome of a decision. 3. Working Principle Select the best feature to split the dataset using a criterion (e.g., Gini Index, Entropy, Information Gain). Split the dataset into subsets based on the chosen feature. Repeat the process recursively for each subset until: All records in a node belong to the same class, or There are no remaining features, or The maximum depth is reached. Assign the majority class (or mean value in regression) to the leaf node.

Post-Pruning: Grow the full tree, then remove unnecessary branches.

TY.BSc.CS Semester V Omkar Madyal Roll No : 00 Artificial Intelligence Page 2 of PRACTICAL NO 1 Breadth First Search & Iterative Depth First Search Implement the Breadth First Search algorithm to solve a given problem Breadth-First Search (BFS) is a fundamental algorithm used to traverse a tree in a level-wise manner. In this method, nodes are visited one level at a time, starting from the root node, then moving on to all nodes at the next level, and so on until every node in the tree has been visited. The traversal begins at the root node, which is the topmost node in the tree. From the root, the algorithm first visits all immediate child nodes. Once all nodes at the current level are processed, the traversal continues to the nodes at the next level. This process continues level by level until all nodes have been visited. BFS is implemented using a queue data structure, which follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle. At the beginning of the traversal, the root node is inserted into the queue. Then, in a loop, the node at the front of the queue is removed (dequeued), processed, and its children are added (enqueued) to the end of the queue. This ensures that nodes are processed in the exact order they appear level by level in the tree. One of the key benefits of BFS in trees is that it does not require tracking visited nodes, because in a tree, each node is unique and there are no repeated connections or cycles. This makes BFS implementation in trees simpler and more efficient compared to other structures. The time complexity of BFS in a tree is O(n), where n is the number of nodes in the tree. This is because each node is visited exactly once. The space complexity is also O(n) in the worst case, especially when the tree is wide and a large number of nodes need to be stored in the queue at the same time (for example, all nodes at the bottom level). BFS is particularly useful when solving problems that involve:  Visiting nodes in level order  Finding the minimum number of steps from the root to a particular node  Determining the height or depth of a tree  Collecting or printing nodes grouped by level Applications of BFS File System Browsers (Windows Explorer, macOS Finder) Operating systems organize files and directories in a tree-like structure, where each folder is a node, and subfolders or files are its children. Introduction AdaBoost, short for Adaptive Boosting, is a powerful ensemble learning technique introduced by Yoav Freund and Robert Schapire in 1996. It is one of the first boosting algorithms that gained popularity due to its simplicity and effectiveness. AdaBoost combines multiple weak learners (usually decision stumps) to form a strong learner with high predictive accuracy. 2. Concept of Ensemble Learning Ensemble learning is based on the principle that combining the predictions of multiple models can result in better performance than any individual model. There are three main types of ensemble methods: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) – e.g., Random Forest Boosting – e.g., AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost Stacking – combining predictions of different model types AdaBoost falls under the Boosting category, where weak learners are trained sequentially, and each new learner focuses more on the mistakes made by the previous ones. 3. Idea Behind AdaBoost The idea of AdaBoost is to: Train multiple weak learners one after another. Assign weights to each training sample. In each iteration, increase the weight of misclassified samples so that the next model pays more attention to them. Combine all weak learners using a weighted majority vote (for classification) or weighted average (for regression). 4. Working of AdaBoost (Step-by-Step) Let’s assume we are solving a binary classification problem. Step 1: Initialize Weights

Instead, it memorizes the dataset and makes predictions based on the nearest neighbors at query time.It is a non-parametric algorithm, meaning it makes no assumptions about the underlying data distribution. Basic Idea To classify a new data point, the algorithm: Finds the K nearest data points in the training set (using distance measures like Euclidean distance). Looks at the labels of those K neighbors. Assigns the label that is most frequent among them (majority voting). For regression, it takes the average (or weighted average) of the K neighbors’ values.

TY.BSc.CS Semester V Omkar Madyal Roll No : 00 Artificial Intelligence Page 4 of Implement the Iterative Depth First Search algorithm to solve the same problem Iterative Depth-First Search (DFS) is a graph or tree traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, but instead of using recursion, it uses an explicit stack data structure to manage traversal order. This makes the algorithm iterative in nature, as it avoids relying on the system's call stack. In traditional DFS, recursion is commonly used to move deeper into the structure, which implicitly makes use of the call stack to remember the previous states. However, recursion can lead to problems such as stack overflow in deep or large graphs. The iterative approach solves this problem by replacing the function call stack with a user-defined stack data structure, which gives more control and safety during traversal. The algorithm starts by pushing the starting node onto the stack. While the stack is not empty, the algorithm pops the top node, processes it, and then pushes all its unvisited neighbors onto the stack. To prevent visiting the same node multiple times (especially in graphs), a visited set or array is maintained. Since the stack operates in Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) order, the last neighbor added to the stack is processed first. This behavior enables the algorithm to dive deep into the structure before returning to explore other branches — which is the essence of depth-first search. In the case of trees, where there are no cycles, maintaining a visited array is usually unnecessary. But in graphs, it is essential to avoid infinite loops caused by cycles or repeated nodes. Working Steps of Iterative DFS: Create an empty stack and push the starting node onto it. Mark the starting node as visited. While the stack is not empty: Pop the top node from the stack. Process the node (e.g., print its value). For each adjacent or child node of the current node: If the node is not already visited: Mark it as visited. Push it onto the stack. Time and Space Complexity: Time Complexity: O(V + E) where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges. Each node and edge is processed once. Space Complexity: O(V) in the worst case, for storing the stack and visited list. Advantages of Iterative DFS: Avoids function call stack overflow that occurs in recursive DFS. Gives more control over traversal, especially in complex graph structures.

While they may appear similar in terms of implementation, their execution order, memory usage, and practical applications differ significantly. Below is a detailed comparison based on various factors: 1. Traversal Order BFS visits nodes level by level, starting from the root or source node and exploring all neighbors before moving deeper. Iterative DFS explores nodes as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack to manage the traversal path. BFS provides a broader view; DFS dives deep into one path before exploring others. 2. Data Structure Used BFS uses a Queue (FIFO) to ensure level-wise traversal. Iterative DFS uses a Stack (LIFO) to simulate the recursive behavior of standard DFS. 3. Time Complexity Both algorithms have similar time complexity in most cases: BFS: O(V + E) Iterative DFS: O(V + E) Where: V is the number of vertices (nodes) E is the number of edges. In terms of raw execution time, neither is significantly faster. Efficiency depends more on the structure of the data and the problem requirements. 4. Space Complexity BFS: O(V) in the worst case — the queue can grow large if the tree/graph is wide. Iterative DFS: O(V) in the worst case — the stack may grow large in deep trees or graphs. DFS is usually more memory-efficient for deep and narrow trees. BFS may require more memory when many nodes exist at the same depth. 5. Shortest Path Finding BFS guarantees the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

TY.BSc.CS Semester V Omkar Madyal Roll No : 00 Artificial Intelligence Page 7 of Iterative DFS does not guarantee the shortest path as it may find a deeper path first. BFS is preferred for shortest path problems. While BFS and Iterative DFS have similar time complexity, their performance and efficiency vary based on the problem context. BFS is better suited for level-based exploration and shortest-path problems, whereas Iterative DFS is ideal for deep exploration, structural analysis, and solving puzzles or backtracking-based problems. Understanding the nature of the input data and the specific requirements of the problem is essential in choosing the most appropriate traversal method.

is

Breadth-First Search (BFS)	algorithm used to traverse a
tree in a	level-wise manner.	In this
method, nodes are visited one level at a time, starting from the root node, then moving on to all nodes at the next level,			
and so on until every node in the tree has been visited.			
The traversal begins at the root node, which is the topmost node in the tree. From the root, the algorithm first visits all			
immediate child nodes. Once all nodes at
the current	level are processed,	the traversal continues to the nodes at	the
next level. This process continues level by level until all nodes have been visited.			
BFS is implemented using a queue data structure, which follows	the First-In-First-Out	(FIFO) principle. At	the
beginning of the traversal, the root node is inserted into the queue. Then, in a loop, the node at the front of the queue is			
removed (dequeued), processed, and its children are added (enqueued) to the end of the queue. This ensures that nodes			
are processed in the exact order they appear level by level in the tree.			
One of the key benefits of BFS in trees is that it does not require tracking visited nodes, because in a tree, each node			
is unique and there are no repeated connections or cycles. This makes BFS implementation in trees simpler and more			
efficient compared to other structures.			
The time complexity of BFS in a tree is O(n), where n is the number of nodes in the tree. This is because each node is			
visited exactly once. The space complexity is also O(n) in the worst case, especially when the tree is wide and a large			
number of nodes need to be stored in the queue at the same time (for example, all nodes at the bottom level).

(KNN)
supervised machine

algorithm used
classification
regression.It is a lazy learner (no explicit training phase). Instead, it memorizes the dataset and makes predictions
based on the nearest neighbors at query time.It
is a non-parametric algorithm, meaning it makes no assumptions
about the underlying data distribution.
Basic Idea
To classify a new data point, the algorithm:
Finds the K nearest data points in the training set (using distance measures like Euclidean distance).
Looks at the labels of those K neighbors.
Assigns the label that is most frequent among them (majority voting).
For regression, it takes the average (or weighted average) of the K neighbors’ values.

Implement the Iterative Depth First Search algorithm to solve the same problem
Iterative Depth-First Search (DFS) is a graph or tree traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each
branch before backtracking, but instead of using recursion, it uses an explicit stack data structure to manage traversal
order. This makes the algorithm iterative in nature, as it avoids relying on the system's call stack.
In traditional DFS, recursion is commonly used to move deeper into the structure, which implicitly makes use of the
call stack to remember the previous states. However, recursion can lead to problems such as stack overflow in deep or
large graphs. The iterative approach solves this problem by replacing the function call stack with a user-defined stack
data structure, which gives more control and safety during traversal.
The algorithm starts by pushing the starting node onto the stack. While the stack is not empty, the algorithm pops the
top node, processes it, and then pushes all
its unvisited neighbors onto the stack. To prevent visiting the same node
multiple times (especially in graphs), a visited set or array is maintained.
the last neighbor added to the stack is processed first.
Since the stack operates in Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) order,
This behavior enables
the algorithm to dive deep into the structure before returning to explore other branches —
which is the essence of depth-first search.
it is
In the case of trees, where there are no cycles, maintaining a visited array is usually unnecessary. But
in graphs,
essential to avoid infinite loops caused by cycles or repeated nodes.

1. Traversal Order

Iterative DFS does not guarantee the shortest path as it may find a deeper path first.
BFS is preferred for shortest path problems.

time complexity,

problem context. BFS is better suited for level-based exploration and shortest-path problems, whereas Iterative DFS is
ideal for deep exploration, structural analysis, and solving puzzles or backtracking-based problems. Understanding the
